title: Why this file exists
trigger: Rahul, after reviewing the first redesigned calculator screen: feedback about spirit was being acted on but not recorded, so it survived only as long as the conversation did.
verbatim: i hope every feed back i give is recorded in spirit so that it remains material and effective for everything we do. because we are designing a system and most of my feedback will be about the spirit we should follow and i may not be able to reproduce a good feedback everytime, but we must move forward not run on a treadmill... we are running towards a goal and the most important part is to make sure that our list of failure has no repetitions and once we learn a lesson it becomes our guide for the future and the lesson may come out of a small thing but the spirit underneath it may apply to everything
spirit: Engineering faults go to engineering-solutions.json. Content faults go to failure_log.jsonl. Judgment about SPIRIT had no home, so it lived in conversation and died with it. This file is that home. A lesson is only learned once it stops being re-learnable.
rules: Record the spirit, not just the fix. The instance is the occasion; the principle is the asset.
Preserve the verbatim words. Rahul's phrasing carries nuance that a paraphrase loses, and he may not reproduce it as well a second time.
A principle that cannot be checked will be violated again. Every entry carries a test.
The lesson may arrive attached to something small. Its scope is not the size of its trigger.

Run the tests BEFORE designing, not after building. Every entry's `test` is a question to be answered on paper while the thing is still cheap to change. Recording a lesson and then designing without consulting it is the same failure as never recording it, and it is how a doctrine becomes an archive.

Promises do not survive. Every rule here that has been broken twice must be given a mechanism that makes breaking it visible - a test, a required artefact, a gate - not a firmer intention. Two rules reached that threshold on 15 Aug: running the doctrine checks before designing, and updating the Launch Gate in the same turn as a change of plan.
do: Record the spirit in this file BEFORE acting on the feedback.
Keep the verbatim words exactly, spelling and punctuation included.
Give every entry a test that can be answered on paper.
Answer the relevant tests before designing, while the design is still cheap to change.
Treat a small trigger as evidence of a principle that may govern everything.
dont: Don't paraphrase, tidy or shorten the verbatim quote.
Don't act first and record afterwards.
Don't answer a twice-broken rule with a firmer intention instead of a mechanism.
Don't treat a recorded lesson as a filed one; an unconsulted doctrine is an archive.
test: Before any design or UX decision this file is read, and each relevant entry's test is answered explicitly for the thing being designed. Any principle here violated twice is a process failure, not a mistake.

title: The offering is all the complexity, packaged - never reduced
trigger: Clarifying the purpose of the whole product while reviewing the calculator redesign.
verbatim: our audience is the lay person but our product and offering is all the complexities in the world, not reduced not diluted not stripped down, packaged in a way that it becomes available, accessible and affordable to our user
spirit: Simplicity here is a property of DELIVERY, not of content. Nothing is removed, softened, or dumbed down. The layperson gets the whole of it - the difficulty lives in the packaging, which is our work, not theirs. This is the operational meaning of 'it is so simple to be difficult but it is so difficult to be simple': the difficulty is ours to absorb.
corrects: sol-019's 'three inputs' rule, which could be misread as reduction. Three inputs is the ENTRY, not the offering. Everything else must remain present and reachable - moved, never deleted.
do: Move complexity to a deeper layer and keep it reachable.
Absorb the difficulty of packaging into our work, never the reader's.
Within a filtered set, offer every eligible option rather than a curated shortlist.
dont: Don't delete a capability in order to make a screen simpler.
Don't read 'three inputs' as the offering; it is the entry only.
test: For any simplification, ask: did the complexity move, or did it disappear? If a capability is no longer reachable by a determined user, this has been violated.

reinforced.context: The note at the foot of Rahul's tax-calculator UI sketch, specifying what the two dropdowns must contain. Transcribed in docs/sketches/tax-calculator-ui_2026-08-16.md.
reinforced.verbatim: The dropdowns will have exhaustive sources of money & deductions category wise. The mechanics underneath will be complex & would clash but the UI to be simple & easy & intuitive.
reinforced.note: Recorded against dd-001 rather than as a new entry: this is dd-001 applied to one screen, and a duplicated rule weakens both copies - the next builder would have to work out which of the two governs. It does add one operational requirement that dd-001 did not state outright, so that is extracted as a `do` below: EXHAUSTIVE within the eligible set. Read with dd-020 it completes the contract - dd-020 says what a category may remove (only the inapplicable), this says how full what remains must be (everything).

title: Layer by the user's next question, not by volume of content
trigger: The first redesigned SWP screen. Layer 1 was three questions; opening the next layer exposed the entire original page at once.
verbatim: the transition from the minimal UI to the complexities has to be layered and more nuanced and the user has to be hand held throughout the way... its like at one moment we are teaching the user the A,B,C and the very next moment they are exposed to the shakesperian or aristotalian level dense prose to parse
spirit: Progressive disclosure measured in quantity revealed is not layering - it relocates the wall. Layers must follow the questions a user is actually having, in the order they have them. Each layer answers ONE question, exposes ONE control, shows ONE consequence, and hands off to the next question. A person who has just been taught the alphabet cannot be handed Aristotle.
note: This is sol-008's constructivism applied to interface instead of prose: people absorb concepts they construct, not concepts delivered to them. The article doctrine already knew this; the UI had not inherited it.
do: Open each layer on one question the reader is actually having, in the order they have it.
Expose one control and one consequence per step, then hand off to the next question.
dont: Don't measure layering by the volume of content revealed.
Don't reveal more than about two new controls or concepts in a single step.
test: Count the controls and new concepts revealed by a single disclosure step. More than about two means the step is a cliff. Every step must be answerable: which question of the user's does this answer?

title: The user pays in time and attention
trigger: Defining what value from a calculator actually means.
verbatim: How i define value derived from this calculator: not what it is capable of, thats the non-negotiable infra (the features and the absolutely correct and empirically verifiable calculation and results) but whether it can get to the user's mind and reserve mindspace for itself, become a tool for the user, like bicycle for the mind... the user pays us in the currency of their time and attention
spirit: Capability is the floor, not the product. Correct maths and full features are the price of admission, not the achievement. The achievement is that the user leaves able to think about the problem - carrying a transferable intuition rather than a number and a dependency. A tool that is used once and never re-enters the mind has failed even if every figure it printed was right.
consequence: Every screen is charged for. If a screen costs thirty seconds of attention and leaves nothing the user can carry away and use, we have taken payment and delivered nothing.
do: Give every screen one transferable idea the reader could use without us.
Treat correct maths and full features as the price of admission.
dont: Don't let a screen's only takeaway be a number.
Don't mistake capability for achievement.
test: For every screen: what idea does the user leave with that they did not arrive with, and could they now use it without us? If the honest answer is 'a number', that screen has taken payment without delivering.

title: Never use a concept the reader has not been given
trigger: The money-flow rung mixed today's money and future rupees, and reconciled them in a closing line that assumed the reader already knew the distinction.
verbatim: One thing that confuses me, when i am looking at a number is it real or nominal ? Are we assuming that a reader knows about real and nominal ? ... it is not clear that: the 1.57 crore left is the purchasing power or the amount of money left in corpus after 30 years ?
spirit: A distinction the reader does not hold cannot be resolved by a footnote. If two number systems appear on a screen, the difference between them is itself an idea and earns its own step - it is never a parenthetical. Reconciling in passing looks like rigour and reads like noise.
rules: Every figure carries its frame visibly and permanently, not in a caption the eye skips.

Default to the reader's native units. A person knows what Rs 40,000 a month buys today; nobody has intuition for Rs 2.3 lakh a month in 2056. Today's money is the default; future rupees are the thing you opt into.
Teach the distinction before relying on it, on its own step, in the reader's words - not 'real and nominal'.
do: Carry each figure's frame on the figure itself, visibly and permanently.
Default to today's money; make future rupees the thing the reader opts into.
Teach a distinction on its own step, in the reader's words, before relying on it.
dont: Don't reconcile two number systems in a footnote, caption or parenthetical.
Don't use the words real and nominal as if the reader already holds them.
test: Point at any number on any screen. Can the reader say which money it is in, without scrolling and without knowing the words real or nominal? If not, this is violated.

title: Find the one comparison the whole subject reduces to
trigger: Asking what the corpus actually has to survive - inflation, withdrawals, corrections, capital gains tax, optional hedging premiums - and still compound.
verbatim: it is not clear that: if inflation is eroding my real value by 6% every year and i withdrew 6%, then at what rate is my corpus growing ? maybe 1-2% real rate of return. ... corpus has to survive inflation, monthly withdrawal, occational market correction or recession, capital gain taxes, maybe insurance premiums if the user chooses and still compound that has to be explained to the user too but without any cognitive load.
spirit: A long list of things to worry about is cognitive load. The same list, expressed as pressure on ONE comparison, is a mental model. For withdrawal planning that comparison is: what the pot really grows at, against what you are really taking out. Every other factor - tax, fees, inflation, hedging premium, a crash - is a force pushing one of those two numbers. Show the comparison, then let each concern arrive as a push on it, and the reader assembles the whole picture without carrying a list.
note: This is what 'bicycle for the mind' (dd-003) looks like in practice. The reader who leaves holding one comparison can reason about products we have never built; the reader who leaves holding seven caveats has memorised our screen.
do: Name the single comparison the whole subject reduces to, and put it on screen.
Introduce every other factor as a push on one side of that comparison.
dont: Don't hand the reader a list of things to worry about and call it completeness.
test: For any calculator, name the single comparison it reduces to. If there isn't one, the model has not been found yet and the screen is still a list.

title: Never make the reader diff two states
trigger: The what-it-buys / what-the-statement-says toggle. Flipping it rewrote three paragraphs in which most words were identical and a few numbers changed mid-sentence.
verbatim: when i switch from one toggle to other and vice versa, i encounter cognitive load, as majority of the text stays the same and something in the middle of the text changes, i am challenged to find out what changes with the toggle... Now it is a lot of cognitive work to find out what changed and that is a problem for me.
spirit: A control that swaps one body of text for a nearly identical one hands the reader a spot-the-difference puzzle and calls it a feature. Holding state A in memory to compare against state B is the most expensive thing an interface can ask for. When two views of the same thing both matter, SHOW BOTH, adjacent, so the comparison is free. A toggle is only honest when the two states are genuinely alternatives the reader chooses between - never when the difference between them is itself the point.
note: The irony recorded for the future: the gap between the two figures had already been identified as the most valuable fact on the screen, and then half of it was hidden behind a control. If a difference is the lesson, it cannot be a mode.
do: Show both views adjacently when both of them matter.
Reserve a toggle for genuine alternatives the reader is choosing between.
dont: Don't swap one body of text for a nearly identical one.
Don't hide half of a difference behind a control when the difference is the lesson.
test: Flip the control and watch your own eyes. If you have to hunt for what changed, the reader will fail where you merely struggled. Prefer adjacency to alternation.

title: Every visual difference must mean something
trigger: Three stacked paragraphs in the money-flow rung, each set smaller than the one above it, with no rule behind the sizing.
verbatim: the result displays three cascading sections of text, each gets progressively smaller in font size, what does that indicate ? is the progressive text less important, what does the change in font size really trying to communicate to the reader ? I am not clear about it.
spirit: Size, weight, colour and order are claims about importance, and a reader decodes them whether or not anything was meant. A cascade of shrinking paragraphs asserts a hierarchy that does not exist, so the reader spends attention working out a rule that was never there. If three things matter equally they look equal; if one matters more it is alone. Decorative hierarchy is not neutral - it is a false statement rendered in typography.
do: State what each difference in size, weight or colour asserts.
Make equal things look equal; isolate the one thing that matters more.
dont: Don't cascade font sizes because it looks better.
Don't render a hierarchy that does not exist.
test: For each difference in size, weight or colour on a screen, state what it asserts. If the answer is 'it looked better', remove it and make the elements equal.

title: A control changes what you SEE, never what you have to RE-READ
trigger: Rungs 3-5 are all 'what if X changes', which implies a slider - but a slider that rewrites a paragraph is dd-006 in slow motion, and there are far too many positions to write prose for.
verbatim: i want controls so the user can interact with it, but i understand the text can not change with every permutation and combination as they would be many many such combinations, we have to find an ingenious way out of this conundrum and we have to innovate our way out of this.
spirit: The conundrum dissolves once prose and values are given different jobs. Prose carries principles, which are true at every position of every control and therefore never change. Values live in fixed positions - a table cell, a gauge, a marker on a track - where a change is SEEN as a digit ticking or a bar moving, not READ as a sentence rewritten. Nothing that moves has to be re-read, and nothing that must be read ever moves.
rules: Prose states the principle, never the current value. 'The rate you draw matters more than the amount you start with' is true at every slider position, so dragging cannot invalidate it.
Live values sit in fixed slots. The eye returns to the same place and sees a number change there - which is free - instead of scanning a paragraph for what is different, which is not.

State the BOUNDARY, not the state. Do not describe where the reader currently is; name where it breaks - 'this plan needs growth above 9.8% to keep working'. One sentence covers the entire range of the control, and it only changes when some OTHER input changes.
Mark the boundary on the control itself. A notch on the track means the reader crosses a visible line as they drag, and learns the threshold without reading anything at all.
note: This is the constructive form of dd-006. That entry said do not make the reader diff two states; this says how to build a control that never produces a diff in the first place.
do: Put live values in fixed slots the eye can return to.
Write prose as principles that stay true at every position of every control.
State the boundary — where the plan breaks — instead of the current state.
Mark that boundary on the control's own track.
dont: Don't rewrite a sentence as a control moves.
Don't describe where the reader currently is.
test: Drag the control from one end to the other. Does any sentence change? If yes, that sentence was describing a state rather than a principle or a boundary, and it belongs in a fixed slot as a value instead.

title: Simplicity is removing WORK, not removing INFORMATION
trigger: Rung 4 showed a -30% year without ever saying what a bad year is, and displayed a 10.60% average against a stated 12% assumption without explaining the difference.
verbatim: it reduces the cognitive load by reducing information available to absorb but introduces cognitive load again by skipping important information required to fully comprehand what is being communicated... we didn't define "what is a bad year"... When we assumed 12% returns then why are we displaying 10.6% average returns without informing the user about this decision; creates a disconnect and user's brain has to process more than they should, tool should process, user should only digest or abosrb and have his doubts cleared not have more doubts along the way.
spirit: Cutting an explanation makes the screen shorter and the reader's job harder. Every unexplained number is a question handed to the reader, and questions are the expensive thing - not words. A shorter screen that provokes 'wait, why 10.6?' has not reduced load, it has moved load off the page and into the reader's head where we cannot see it. This is dd-001 at the scale of a single screen: the complexity must be absorbed, not deleted.
rules: Every number on screen must be traceable from what is already on screen. If a figure differs from an assumption stated elsewhere, say why, there, in the same breath.
Name the thing before using it. A '-30% year' means nothing until the reader is told what that is and how often it happens.
The tool does the processing; the reader does the absorbing. Any arithmetic the reader has to perform to follow the argument is arithmetic we failed to do.
do: Make every number traceable from what is already on the screen.
Name a thing, and how often it happens, before using it.
Do the arithmetic for the reader; the tool processes, the reader absorbs.
dont: Don't show a figure that differs from a stated assumption without saying why, in the same breath.
Don't shorten a screen by deleting an explanation.
test: Read the screen as someone who knows nothing. Count the questions it raises that it does not answer. That count is the real cognitive load, and it is not reduced by having fewer words.
verbatim_note: Recorded exactly as written, spelling included. An earlier version silently corrected 'comprehand' and 'abosrb'. Tidying a record is editing it, and the point of keeping the words is that they are his and not mine.
relationship: Not a new principle. This is dd-001 - complexity is packaged, never reduced - applied at the scale of a single screen. dd-001 was read as being about features; explanations are complexity too. Recorded as a restatement rather than a discovery, because pretending it is new hides that an existing principle was available and went unapplied.

title: Measure the lived experience, not the accountant's summary
trigger: Rung 4 reported the final balance after 30 years as its headline outcome.
verbatim: if it means what the user ends up with after 30 years of withdrawing what he wanted, it needs to be made more explicit that one bad year doesn't jeopardize their ability to maintain their standard of living... but that is in hindsight, but it affects their stress level along the way of those 30 years, that is a more intimate lived reality.
spirit: Nobody experiences a terminal balance. A retiree experiences thirty years of wondering whether the money will hold - and the year the pot dipped closest to the edge is felt far more sharply than the number left over at the end. A final figure is the correct answer to an accountant's question and the wrong answer to a person's. Choose the quantity a human actually lives through, then let the summary figure sit beside it as context.
note: Distinct from dd-003. That entry asks what idea the reader leaves with; this asks which QUANTITY to put on screen. A number can be perfectly accurate, perfectly explained, and still be about the wrong thing.
do: Headline the quantity a person actually lives through, month to month.
Let the summary figure sit beside it as context.
dont: Don't headline a terminal balance, or any other accountant's summary.
test: Ask what the person would actually feel, month to month, living inside this projection. If the headline figure is not something they would ever experience, it is the wrong headline.

title: A record with no failure mode will drift, and an expensive record will be skipped
trigger: The Launch Gate fell two commits behind within two hours of a protocol saying it must be updated in the same turn - and I had written that protocol.
verbatim:
why did this happen and how to prevent, you from breaking your own rule, from happening again?

[on being told the gate was expensive to maintain] "I dont want to spend more tokens that i have to to update the launch gate? you should have told me before. I need it to track progress but it has to be low cost and frugal i.e. the launchgate, it is just a dynamic task list."
spirit:
Discipline is not what keeps records current; consequences are. Every store that held up under pressure had a way of breaking loudly when neglected - a commit needs a message, a ratchet turns the suite red, an invariant fails. The Launch Gate had only an intention, lived outside the repository where git could not see it, and therefore aged in silence. Nothing detected it because nothing could.

The second cause is quieter and just as real: the gate was six hundred lines of hand-patched HTML, so every update was a tax. Expensive obligations get rationalised away at the end of long turns, exactly when fatigue is highest and the work feels finished. Making the right thing cheap is not a convenience, it is a control.
rules: Every durable store gets a detector. If neglecting it produces no signal, it will be neglected - not through carelessness but because nothing distinguishes the neglected state from the healthy one.
The detector names what is missing and what to do, not merely that something is wrong. A red light with no address gets muted.
Keep the record where the tooling can see it. A file outside the repository cannot be checked by anything the repository runs.
Reduce the cost of compliance. If updating a record is laborious, the laboriousness is a cause of the drift and fixing it is part of the fix.
Restating a rule more firmly is not a mechanism. That had already been tried once, on dd-000, and failed within a day.

Say what a thing will cost to maintain, before building it. An artefact that is expensive to keep current spends the user's tokens on every future turn, and that is their decision to make, not ours to absorb silently. The Launch Gate was built as a designed document when a list was asked for; nobody chose that cost, it was simply incurred.
note: Written after the second process failure of the same session. The first was skipping the doctrine checks before rung 4; the second was this. Both were answered with intentions before they were answered with tests, and only the tests held.
applies_to: any record we intend to keep current
do: Give every durable store a detector that names what is missing and what to do.
Keep the record inside the repository, where the tooling can see it.
Reduce the cost of compliance; laboriousness is itself a cause of drift.
Say what an artefact will cost to maintain before building it.
dont: Don't answer a broken rule by restating it more firmly.
Don't build a designed document when a list was asked for.
test: For each store we rely on: what breaks, visibly, if it is neglected for a week? If the answer is 'nothing', it is already drifting and we simply cannot see it yet.

title: Judge a thing by the situation it exists for, not by an average over all situations
trigger: Rung 5 reported protection as a change in survival averaged over all 10,000 futures - "95 in 100 unprotected, 93 in 100 protected" - and a difference row reading "− 2 in 100".
verbatim:
I didn't understand what it means "futures in 100 where the money last all 30 years" unprotected and protected ? how is unprotected futures more probable than protected futures. I mean the insurance is not there to increase the probability of corpus lasting full 30 years, it is there to prevent it from not lasting 30 years in futures where the bad years appear. it is not very intuitive and frankly put a lot of cognitive load on the user and may want one to quit using our product all together.

A scenario: where bad years are consecutive then for every year i loose maximum 10% or anywhere between 1 to 10 % eventhough the market may have lost more but i loose despite paying premium for protection, this makes the 10% floor a hard sell.

The "So protection is worth -4 in 100" makes no sense to a lay person. this is the worst example of not learning from our own failures and the best example of keeping the user scratching his head in confusion.
spirit:
Insurance does not exist to raise an average. It exists for the minority of futures where things go wrong, and it is paid for out of all the others. Reporting it as a movement in an all-futures average therefore judges it by the one measure it was never built to move, and the honest arithmetic then reads as an argument against the product - which is both confusing and beside the point.

The reader's question is not "does this raise my odds". It is "when the bad years come, what happens to me with this and without it". Show those futures. The average over everything is the accountant's summary again, one level up from the terminal balance dd-010 already rejected.

And a difference of averages - "− 2 in 100" - is worse than the averages themselves. It is a number with no referent in anything the reader can picture. A quantity nobody could ever experience cannot be the verdict line of a screen.
repeat_violations: This is not a new lesson, which is the part that matters. "− 2 in 100" is dd-009: a figure the screen does not let the reader trace. Leading with an all-futures average is dd-010: the summary rather than the lived thing. Both were recorded the same day, both were cited in the rung's own checks file, and both were violated anyway - so the checks were answered on paper without being applied. Per dd-000 that is a process failure, not a mistake.
rules: Show the thing in the situation it exists for. For protection that means the bad futures - the worst decile, the sequence-risk case - not the mean over all of them.
Never headline a difference of two averages. If the reader cannot picture one instance of the quantity, it cannot carry the verdict.

State what a protection does NOT cover as plainly as what it does. An annual floor does nothing about consecutive bad years - three years at -10% is -27% - and the reader must learn that from us rather than discover it later.
A screen that leaves the reader scratching their head has failed even if every figure on it is correct. Confusion is a defect of the same class as a wrong number.
applies_to: any feature that exists for the tail
do: Show the feature in the situation it exists for — for protection, the bad futures.
State as plainly what a protection does not cover as what it does.
dont: Don't headline an average taken over situations the feature was never meant to affect.
Don't make a difference of two averages the verdict line.
Don't ship a screen that leaves the reader confused, however correct its figures.
test: Name the situation the feature exists for. Is that situation on the screen? If the headline is an average taken over all situations, including the many the feature was never meant to affect, the wrong measure is being reported. And point at the verdict line: can the reader picture a single concrete instance of that quantity? If not, replace it.

title: One engine. Two surfaces may never show different numbers for the same input
trigger: The ladder and the advanced panel on the same page, at the same inputs, disagreed: tax of Rs 36.9 L against Rs 38.51 L, an end balance of Rs 17.15 cr against Rs 17.02 cr, spending of Rs 3.38 cr against a gross of Rs 3.79 cr. The three entry inputs at the top of the page did not drive the advanced panel at all.
verbatim:
The input figures in the first rung are not used in the advanced mode, advanced mode used its own inputs ???

The advanced mode figures and rung 3 figures don't match. There can be no bigger failure than this. have you abandoned the advanced mode entirely ? it was understood that the same underlysing infra would be used, how come i see two different sort of numbers for the same input ?

I am utterly dissappointed after working for the whole day, i have found so many calculation errors and despite stressing on user friendliness with low cognitive load, i find the same failures repeated.
spirit:
A calculator that shows a reader two different answers to one question has destroyed the only thing it was selling. Correct arithmetic is the floor, not the achievement (dd-003) - and two correct-looking answers that disagree are worse than one wrong one, because the reader cannot tell which to believe and now cannot trust either. Everything the ladder was built to teach is worthless the moment the panel below it contradicts it.

The cause is always the same shape: a new surface is built beside the old one instead of on top of it. The ladder got its own worker, its own inputs, its own simulation count and seed; the advanced panel kept its own. Nobody decided they should differ. They were simply never made to be the same thing, and no test asked.

This is sol-023 at the scale of a page rather than a table. That entry's rule - a view must never re-derive what the engine already knows - was written about a ledger. It was always about every surface.
rules: One computation per set of inputs, and every surface subscribes to it. Not "the same function called twice" - the same result, distributed.
Inputs are entered once. A second set of fields for the same quantity is a second source of truth and will drift within a day.
When a simple view and an expert view coexist, the simple one is a projection of the expert one. Building it alongside guarantees divergence; building it on top makes divergence impossible.
A shared number gets a test that asserts the two surfaces agree. Agreement that rests on both being written correctly is not agreement, it is a coincidence with a deadline.
applies_to: any page with more than one view of the same computation
do: Compute once per set of inputs and distribute that one result to every surface.
Build the simple view as a projection of the expert one.
Assert in a test that the two surfaces agree on every shared number.
dont: Don't give a new surface its own inputs, worker, seed or simulation count.
Don't let one quantity appear twice on a page with two values.
test: Change one input and read every figure on the page. Does any quantity appear twice with two values? If two surfaces can be made to disagree by any input, they are two engines and the page is lying to somebody.

title: Use native HTML/CSS for bespoke infographics, not SVGs
trigger: The article 'The Loss That Never Happened' was drafted with [SVG_PROPOSAL] tags instead of actual HTML/CSS components, breaking a previously stated preference.
verbatim: this article neither has hero illustration nor other artifacts and i want html css artifacts not svg, i thought i made this clear a while ago.
spirit: SVGs (or text placeholders for SVGs) are not the FinSight way. The product demands premium, bespoke, responsive infographics built natively with HTML, CSS (Tailwind), and Astro components. A placeholder is a deferred decision; an SVG is often an inflexible asset. We build the interfaces directly in the DOM.
rules: Do not propose or use SVG for infographics. Build them natively as Astro components with HTML/CSS.
Never leave placeholders (like [SVG_PROPOSAL]) in a published or 'finished' article. A draft is not done until the actual visual artifacts are built and wired in.
do: Build infographics natively as Astro components in HTML and Tailwind.
Ship the actual visual artifacts before calling a draft finished.
dont: Don't propose or ship an SVG asset for a bespoke infographic.
Don't leave a placeholder such as [SVG_PROPOSAL] in a finished article.
test: Scan the article for SVGs or placeholders. If the visual explanation relies on an external SVG file or a text placeholder rather than a native HTML/CSS component, this rule has been violated.

title: The Template is the Floor, not the Prose (Bespoke Subheadings and Stealth Learning)
trigger: The content factory generated literal headers like 'TL;DR' and 'First Principles' instead of bespoke narrative propositions.
verbatim: the hook, tldr, origin story, first principles explanation, coverage, mechanism, rupee spine, traps, recourse, key takeaways, disclaimer: this is suppossed to be the minimum floor, we never use these specific sub headings rather we use the idea behind them and use bespoke sub-headings... When i made a rule never to use a few phrases like 'First Principles' we use this as a concept instead . Still this is being used even after i explicitely forbid it.
spirit: Required architectural elements (like a Rupee Spine or a Recourse section) are conceptual checklists, not literal UI headers. The heading must advance the argument (e.g. 'When a Tax Loss Became an Asset') instead of just labeling the section. Explicit meta-language like 'This guide deconstructs...' or 'First Principles' breaks immersion. We teach abstractions layer by layer, by stealth, without announcing the lesson.
rules: Never use internal dossier labels (Hook, Mechanism, Rupee Spine, etc.) as actual MDX headers.
Never use banned phrases like 'First Principles' or 'This guide'. Teach the concept without using the cliché.
Every header must be an editorial proposition that a reader can skim to get the intellectual narrative.
do: Write every header as an editorial proposition that advances the argument.
Treat the dossier sections as a conceptual checklist, a floor to clear.
Teach the abstraction by stealth, layer by layer, without announcing the lesson.
dont: Don't use internal dossier labels (TL;DR, Hook, Mechanism, Rupee Spine) as MDX headers.
Don't use banned meta-language such as 'First Principles' or 'This guide'.
test: Skim only the headers. Do they read like an essay outline (PASS) or a bureaucratic form (FAIL)? Search the text for explicitly banned meta-language; if present, it fails.

title: A lesson is not followable until it has been reduced to do's and don'ts
trigger: Rahul, on being told where his feedback is recorded, immediately proposed the missing half of the mechanism: recording is only the first move, extraction is the second.
verbatim: first: what is the name and path of the file in which my feedback is recorded, i propose a rule after my feedback goes to record and the do and don'ts  and extracted from it and religiously followed. can you do it and setup the mechanics right now
spirit:
This file was built to stop lessons dying in conversation, and it succeeded at that. But it stores them as prose - a trigger, a verbatim quote, a paragraph of reasoning, a test. Prose carries the WHY, which is why it must be kept, and it is exactly the wrong shape for the moment of use. At the moment of designing, what is needed is an instruction: one line, imperative, checkable by someone who has not read the paragraph it came from. A principle that has to be re-derived from an essay each time will be re-derived differently each time, or not at all.

dd-012 is the proof that this gap is real and not theoretical. dd-009 and dd-010 were both recorded, both cited by id in the rung's own checks file, and both violated in that same rung. The citation was honest; it simply was not an instruction. Nothing in 'dd-010' as written told the builder do not headline a difference of two averages - that had to be extracted from a paragraph, and under pressure it was not.

So extraction is not a summary of the doctrine. It is the doctrine in the form that can actually be obeyed, and per dd-011 it needs a mechanism rather than a promise: the entry is invalid without it, the flat list is generated rather than maintained, and the checks files answer don'ts instead of naming entries.
do: Extract the do's and don'ts into the entry itself, in the same turn it is recorded.
Write each line as one imperative that can be checked without reading the entry it came from.
Read the generated docs/doctrine-rules.md before designing anything.
Answer the don'ts that apply, by id, in the component's .checks.md.
dont: Don't record an entry without its do's and don'ts - extraction is part of recording, not a follow-up.
Don't hand-edit docs/doctrine-rules.md; it is a projection of the JSON and dd-013 governs it.
Don't cite an entry in a checks file and leave its don'ts unanswered. That is the dd-012 failure exactly.
Don't write a do or a don't that needs its own paragraph to be understood. If it cannot be a line, it is not yet extracted.
mechanism: src/tests/doctrineRules.test.ts: every entry must carry non-empty do and dont arrays; docs/doctrine-rules.md must be byte-identical to a regeneration (npm run doctrine); every new .checks.md must answer each applicable don't by id with PASS, N/A or RISK; the count of legacy-format checks files is ratcheted and may only fall.
cost: Per new doctrine entry: two to six short lines, written while the lesson is fresh. Per new calculator component: the skeleton is generated by `npm run doctrine:checks <Component>` with every applicable rule pre-filled, so the cost is answering, not typing. The flat list costs nothing - it is generated.
applies_to: every design, UX or copy decision
test: Open docs/doctrine-rules.md. Could a reviewer who has never read the doctrine check a screen against it, line by line? Every entry must appear there with at least one do and one don't, and every checks file must answer the don'ts that apply to it by id.

title: Ask for an input in the same money you report the answer in
trigger: Rahul, on the SIP page's entry contract, after the fund fee had been made visible: the page asks for the goal in today's money and asks for the contribution in plain rupees, and nothing on the page admits the two are different kinds of number.
verbatim:
how about this: and this should have been the first question.

lets give the user answer whether he wants to put a fix sum of money every month
or
a fix percentage of his monthly salary (for salaried)
or
a fixed amount of purchasing power every month (this applies to all)

because their income grows with inflation and more due to their hard work.

what do you think ? i mean the same person after retiring is asking for 50000 per month of purchasing power or real value every month not 50000 rupees every month, its only fair that he invests in the same way.
spirit:
dd-004 was applied to everything the product PRINTS and to nothing it ASKS FOR. The goal is taken in today's money - the field says so, and the tooltip insists a goal in future rupees is not a goal. The retiree's withdrawal is taken in today's money and inflated every year so the purchasing power holds. And then the contribution, which is the input that runs the longest and matters most, is taken as a bare rupee figure that silently decays for the whole horizon.

The asymmetry is not a cosmetic one. A plan that holds the contribution flat in nominal terms is modelling a saver whose real saving falls by about two thirds over twenty years at 6% inflation - somebody getting steadily poorer, aiming at a target defined in money that does not move. Nobody behaves that way and nobody would choose it if asked plainly, and we never asked.

The cause is that the question was put in the unit convenient to the ENGINE - a constant it can multiply twelve times a year - rather than the unit the person thinks in. Rahul's test is symmetry, and it is the right one: the same human being, on the other side of the same product, is asking us for fifty thousand a month of purchasing power. He is not a different person while he is saving.

The wider rule is that an input persisting over time is a rate in disguise, and it carries a frame exactly as an output does. Asking for it without stating the frame does not avoid the assumption; it hides one.
do: Ask for a lasting input in the same money the answer is reported in.
Interpret a monthly contribution as real by default, and say plainly that this is what is being run.
Make a step-up an optional REAL increment for career progression, on top of a base that already holds purchasing power.
Give the salaried a share-of-income framing and the self-employed an inflation-linked one - same arithmetic, two vocabularies.
Show what a real-terms contribution becomes in cash later, so the reader can check they could keep it up.
Treat symmetry with the other side of the product as a design test: would the same person, drawing down, be asked this way?
dont: Don't take a multi-year input as a bare number and let it decay in silence.
Don't put a question in the unit the engine finds convenient rather than the one the reader thinks in.
Don't turn the fix into a mode question at the entry; state the interpretation instead of asking for it.
Don't let a step-up of zero mean the reader's real saving falls every year.
Don't state a goal in today's money beside a contribution in tomorrow's without saying they differ.
relationship: dd-004 applied to the input side. That entry said every figure carries its frame visibly and defaults to the reader's native units, and it was read as being about figures we PRINT. This is the same rule pointed at the fields we ASK. Recorded as an extension rather than a discovery, because pretending it is new would hide that dd-004 was already sufficient and went unapplied for a day.
applies_to: any input that persists over more than a year
test: Read the entry fields and the headline together. Are they in the same money? If the answer is in today's prices and any input is not, name which. And count the questions the entry asks: stating an interpretation is allowed, asking the reader to choose one at step one is not.
refinement_verbatim: fixed purchasing power but frame it so that a salaried person and a self employed or professional (CA, Advocate Doctor) can also connect. I mean the salaried is easy is picture, just a fix percentage of monthly income (this captures inflation) and a stepup is optional but then it won't capture career progression. but for others we have to frame it intelligently and start with sensible defaults like they have to grow their contribution by inflation rate per year and. stepup is optional for them as well. It is best to just think that if the user says 25000 per month they mean 25000 in real terms not nominal terms and just tell them that this is what we are running with. this works for everybody and doesn't introduce cognitive load at the very first step. we can add because you'd want atleast fixed purchasing power post retirement so you have got to invest fixed purchasing power if not a growing purchasing power.
refinement:
Rahul's answer corrected the shape of the fix, not just its default, and the correction is the more important half.

I had proposed the three modes as a QUESTION at the entry - pick how you contribute, then answer the three inputs. He rejected that without naming it: 'this works for everybody and doesn't introduce cognitive load at the very first step'. The entry contract stays three questions (sol-019). What changes is that we INTERPRET the number correctly and say so - if someone types 25,000 a month they mean 25,000 in real terms, and we tell them that is what we are running with. An interpretation stated is not a question asked.

The second correction is structural. A step-up is no longer the nominal growth of the contribution; it is an OPTIONAL REAL increment on top of a base that already holds purchasing power. That separates two things which had been collapsed into one field and were therefore both invisible: keeping pace with prices, which nearly everybody does without thinking, and career progression, which is a genuine extra. At zero step-up the plan now means 'I hold my saving level', not 'I get poorer every year'.

The third is about who the reader is. A fixed percentage of a salary captures inflation by itself, so for the salaried the natural framing is a share of income. A professional in practice - his examples are a CA, an advocate, a doctor - has no payslip, so the same idea has to arrive as growing the contribution with inflation. Same arithmetic, two vocabularies, and picking one for everybody would lose half the audience.

His justification is the sentence to put on the screen, because it is the whole argument in one line: you will want at least fixed purchasing power after you retire, so you have to invest in fixed purchasing power.

title: Flowing prose over choppy sentences
trigger: Rahul comparing the original 'The Price You Didn't Receive' (lots of half a line sentences) with 'The Loss That Never Happened' (proper sentences, paragraphs and flow).
verbatim: compare the two articles 1. The loss that never happened 2. The price you didn't receive. in the 1st article there is flow and proper sentences and paragraphs as compared to the 2nd article where there are a lot of half a line sentences. is it feasible to keep all the content in 2nd article and modify its structure so it feels more like an article. i want you to direct our content factory, and you personally too, to study the two articles ... and draw design, prose, pacing, flow, content, depth, width, language, simplicity, associativeness, intuitiveness, explanability lessons and record them and enforce them.
spirit: FinSight articles are deep-dive, magazine-style whitepapers, not punchy Twitter threads or slide decks. They require flowing, cohesive prose, structured into proper paragraphs that carry a sustained analytical argument. The benchmark is 'The Loss That Never Happened'—which masterfully uses paradoxes, analogies, and pacing to explain complex mechanics. In contrast, the original 'The Price You Didn't Receive' represented the 'lazy AI slop' we must eradicate: it shattered pacing by atomising the text into choppy, single-sentence lines that destroyed perceived authority. The *fixed* version of 'The Price You Didn't Receive' provides our second benchmark: it uses narrative anchoring (Arjun Mehta's startup sale) and explicitly uncovers the 'State's Perspective' (Information Asymmetry) to explain the *why* before the *how*. Simplicity does not mean primitive sentence structure. Intuitiveness and explainability are achieved through narrative flow, associative framing, and clear transitions.
do: Write in flowing, cohesive paragraphs that sustain an analytical argument, matching the pacing of 'The Loss That Never Happened'.
Anchor an abstract tax rule in one named person's concrete conflict, as Section 50CA is anchored in Arjun Mehta's sale.
State the government's own economic motive for a rule - the State's Perspective - not only its mechanics.
Use strong, structural analogies (e.g., slicing a pizza, the 5 share prices) to translate technical depth without losing the reader.
Study 'The Loss That Never Happened' for mechanical pacing and flow.
Study the rewritten 'The Price You Didn't Receive' for narrative anchoring and associative explainability.
dont: Don't write choppy, half-a-line, or single-sentence paragraphs like the original draft of 'The Price You Didn't Receive'.
Don't confuse simplicity of explanation with primitive, staccato sentence structures.
Don't atomise a deep, complex argument into disjointed fragments that destroy the pacing and reading experience.
Don't produce 'lazy AI slop' that blindly lists facts without weaving them into a cohesive, magazine-style narrative.
test: Read the draft aloud. Does it flow like a cohesive, authoritative article in a premium magazine, or does it sound like a disjointed slide presentation? Are the paragraphs properly structured with complete sentences?

title: A number is a quantity, an amount and a frame
trigger: Rahul's ruling on D-2, the open decision raised by the 16 Aug interface audit. The audit proposed four visual rules and could not write any of them as doctrine, because every entry in this file carries Rahul's own words and inventing a quote would corrupt the one store that depends on being real. He ruled on all four in one line.
verbatim: I agree 100% with your recommendation "Take the fourth one at minimum. It generalises the T8 frame work you already did, it is the direct cause of two separate findings, and it is the kind of rule that prevents defects rather than describing them. The other three can live as lint rules without ceremony."
provenance: The sentence Rahul is agreeing to was drafted by the audit, not spoken by him - his verbatim contribution is the ruling itself. Recorded this way on purpose. The alternative was to paraphrase his agreement into first person and present it as his voice, which is the exact failure mode this field exists to prevent. When Rahul ratifies a proposal rather than originating it, the entry says so.
spirit:
T8 was right and incomplete, and the incompleteness is the lesson. T8 established that every projected figure carries its money's frame, and that discipline was applied correctly - to the UNIT. It said nothing about the QUANTITY, so the frame became a label attached to whatever figure was nearby. On the insurance page the phrase 'in today's prices' ended up on at least four different quantities. Two bold figures 500px apart, Rs 9.14 lakh and Rs 9.43 lakh, shared that label while counting entirely different things - the surplus and the total payout - and the reader's first and most reasonable thought is that one is a typo of the other.

A figure is only traceable when the reader can say three things about it without looking anywhere else: what it counts, how much it is, and whose money it is in. All three have to arrive together, as one phrase on one line. Split across a heading, a stat block and a caption, they stop being one number and become three fragments the reader is asked to reassemble - and the reader will not do that work, because CLAUDE.md's whole position is that the difficulty of packaging is ours to absorb and never theirs.

'THE SAME MONEY' as a heading is the sharpest instance: it reads as a claim that two amounts are equal, when what it means is 'this sum, re-expressed'.
do: Write quantity + amount + frame as one phrase on one line, in that order: 'Rs 9.14 lakh more, in today's prices'.
Put the noun that says what a figure counts on the same line as the figure itself.
When two figures on one screen share a frame, make the noun the thing that tells them apart.
Name the quantity even when the frame alone feels sufficient - the unit is not the quantity.
dont: Don't split a number across a label, a stat block and a caption, as in 'THE SAME MONEY / Rs 9.43 Lakh / in today's prices'.
Don't attach the same frame phrase to more than one quantity on a screen without naming each one.
Don't treat a correct frame as sufficient disambiguation; T8 was applied correctly here and the screen was still ambiguous.
Don't use a heading that reads as a claim of equivalence ('THE SAME MONEY') when it means 'this sum, re-expressed'.
test:
Cover the whole screen except the figure and whatever names it. Can the reader say what it counts, how much it is, and in whose money?

A row header naming the quantity and a column header naming the frame BOTH COUNT: that is T8's adjacent-columns pattern, it is the shape dd-006 requires, and it passes. The first draft of this test said 'the line it sits on', which would have condemned every real/nominal table we deliberately built - the wording was the agent's, not Rahul's, and it was wrong.

What fails is a figure whose noun sits in a separate block above it while its frame floats as a caption beside it - and above all, the same frame phrase doing that job for more than one quantity on the same page. That is F-12: two bold figures 500px apart, both labelled 'in today's prices', counting different things.

title: Ask a cheap question to remove what cannot apply - never what is merely unlikely
trigger: Rahul explaining what the Category selector at the top of his tax-calculator sketch is FOR, when asked whether it filters the two dropdowns.
verbatim: Picking a category will not show irrelevant options but the options that are commn across categories should be shown, like picking salaried will not show that they can file return under 44ad or 44ada and claim corresponding under deductions but it will show futures and options as income similar. ctegories use is to remove inapplicable options only so to reduce the cognitive load. a few questions answers from the user can go a long way to reduce cognitive load for the user.
spirit:
The line that carries the whole rule is 'to remove INAPPLICABLE options only'. The filter is eligibility, not likelihood, and the two are constantly confused. A salaried filer cannot elect 44AD or 44ADA - the statute does not permit it - so offering it is pure noise and hiding it costs the reader nothing. A salaried filer absolutely can have futures and options income, and it is not even rare; hiding it because it is uncommon would silently amputate a real user's return and they would never learn what was missing.

So the test on any option is not 'will most people in this category use it?' but 'can a person in this category lawfully use it?' Only the second is a safe reason to remove something. The first is how a form quietly becomes wrong for everyone it did not picture.

The second sentence generalises past the tax page: 'a few questions answers from the user can go a long way to reduce cognitive load'. A small number of cheap questions, asked early, earns the right to remove a large amount of irrelevance later. That is the same bargain as CLAUDE.md's - the difficulty of packaging is ours to absorb, never the reader's - and it is the mechanism by which a page can offer the whole of the complexity (dd-001) without putting all of it on screen at once.
do: Filter an option list by what the reader is ELIGIBLE for, and let everything lawful remain reachable.
Ask a small number of cheap questions early - category, age, status - and spend the answers on removing irrelevance later.
Keep an option that is uncommon but lawful, such as futures and options income for a salaried filer.
Remove an option the reader cannot lawfully choose, such as 44AD or 44ADA for a salaried filer, along with the deductions that depend on it.
dont: Don't hide an option because it is unlikely - unlikely is not inapplicable, and the reader it fits never learns it was there.
Don't ask a question that does not go on to remove something - a question that buys no simplification is pure cost.
Don't let a category filter change a computed answer; it removes what cannot apply, never what is inconvenient to support.
test: Take any option the category has removed and ask: is this removed because the statute forbids it, or because we guessed the reader probably will not need it? Only the first survives. If a salaried reader with F&O income, or a professional with capital gains, would be unable to enter something true about their year, the filter is wrong.
